subject: forensic-medicine
title: Simple Hurt, Antemortem Versus Postmortem Wounds and Age of Injury

steps.title: Simple hurt is what remains
steps.tx: **Simple hurt** is the legal residue: any bodily pain, disease or infirmity inflicted on another that does not fall inside the eight grievous clauses. Abrasions, most contusions and shallow lacerations usually sit here. The grading matters because it drives the charge, the bail position and the compensation conversation. The doctor's duty is accurate description and honest grading, stating the clause relied on whenever grievous hurt is certified.
steps.say: Hurt outside the eight grievous clauses is simple hurt, and the certificate should name the clause whenever grievous is claimed.

rows: Days of pain or lost work

steps.title: Vital reaction proves injury during life
steps.tx: The cornerstone distinction is **vital reaction**: tissues injured during life respond with bleeding into the wound, swelling, congestion, retraction and early cellular infiltration, because circulation and living enzymes still work. After death those responses fail. An antemortem wound therefore shows extravasation and infiltration of blood in its margins, gaping from muscle retraction and blood staining that washing cannot remove. Postmortem wounds look dry, pale or yellow and sharply defined.
steps.say: Bleeding into margins, swelling and gaping mark a wound made in life, while postmortem wounds stay dry and pale.

steps.title: Antemortem versus postmortem abrasions
steps.tx: For abrasions the contrast is visible to the naked eye in **antemortem and postmortem abrasion differences**. Antemortem abrasions are bright reddish brown with more exudation and a scab sitting slightly raised. Postmortem abrasions look yellowish, translucent and parchment like, with the scab lying slightly below skin level, and they favour bony prominences where a dragged body rubs. Microscopy confirms intravital congestion only in the antemortem lesion.
steps.say: Raised reddish scabs anywhere suggest life, while flat parchment abrasions over bony points suggest damage after death.

steps.title: Bruises before and after death
steps.tx: Appreciable bruising needs a beating circulation, so **postmortem bruising** is limited: great violence within two to three hours of death can raise small bruises where tissue is crushed against bone or in hypostatic areas such as the back of the scalp. Antemortem bruises show swelling, damaged epithelium, extravasation, coagulation and colour change, with indistinct margins. Postmortem bruise margins stay sharply defined. In decomposed scalp, haemolysis blurs the distinction badly.
steps.say: Real bruising needs circulation, so only small sharp edged bruises can be forced within two to three hours after death.

steps.title: Ageing a bruise by colour, with caution
steps.tx: Extravasated haemoglobin degrades through a colour parade that roughly gives the **age of a bruise**. Fresh bruises are red, blue within hours to three days, bluish black to brown from haemosiderin on the fourth day, greenish from haematoidin at five to six days, yellow from bilirubin at seven to twelve days, and normal by two weeks. Reddy warns the rate varies widely between persons and even between bruises, so opinions stay cautious.
steps.say: Red, blue, brown, green, yellow dates a bruise across two weeks, but variation is wide and certainty is forbidden.

steps.title: Exceptions that break bruise colour rules
steps.tx: Three exceptions rescue students in viva. **Subconjunctival ecchymosis** never follows the usual colour sequence because oxygen diffuses through the conjunctiva; it stays bright red, then turns yellow directly. Children clear bruises rapidly, sometimes in days, while the elderly heal them very slowly. A bruise raised at the time of carbon monoxide poisoning can stay bright red from carboxyhaemoglobin, imitating a fresh injury on an older body.
steps.say: Eye bruises skip the colour parade, children clear bruises fast, and carbon monoxide keeps a bruise misleadingly red.

steps.title: Ageing incised wounds and lacerations
steps.tx: Cut wounds heal on a timetable usable in court for the **age of an incised wound**. Edges are red, swollen and adherent by twelve hours; a continuous endothelial layer covers the surface by twenty four hours; neutrophils give way to macrophages by seventy two hours; vascularised granulation tissue and new fibrils form at four to five days; a soft reddish scar appears by one week. Lacerations can be aged only when granulation or fibroblast growth shows.
steps.say: Adherent edges at twelve hours, granulation at four days and a soft scar at one week date a healing cut wound.

steps.title: When wounds cannot be separated in time
steps.tx: Honest limits matter: abrasions made slightly before or after death cannot be differentiated even microscopically, and **limits of wound timing** widen as decomposition advances. Blood in wounds of a body immersed soon after injury is lysed by water and washes away, so antemortem and postmortem injuries become indistinguishable. In a decomposed body, even telling a laceration from an incised wound can fail. The report should state these limits instead of guessing.
steps.say: Perimortem scrapes, immersed bodies and decay can erase timing evidence entirely, and the report must admit that plainly.

steps.title: Therapeutic wounds masquerading as trauma
steps.tx: Doctors create wounds that later confuse investigators, grouped as **therapeutic wounds**. Surgical stab wounds for chest drains, laparotomy and thoracotomy incisions, cut downs at wrist, elbow and ankle, and tracheostomy openings can all be mistaken for assault injuries. A drain may even be placed through a homicidal stab wound, merging the two. Hospital records and operation notes, read before the autopsy opinion, prevent this avoidable error.
steps.say: Drain sites, cut downs and tracheostomy wounds imitate assault injuries, so read the treatment records before opining.
